claim: Children in low-income countries often experience infectious diseases and nutritional deficiencies leading to impaired growth, poor development, and early mortality.
source: Children in low-income countries often experience infectious diseases and nutritional deficiencies leading to impaired growth, poor development, and early mortality (Black et al., 2017; GBD 2015 Mortality and Causes of Death Collaborators, 2016; Victora et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by three citations to published literature

claim: During early life, children exhibit heightened developmental plasticity and are more sensitive to environmental conditions than later in life.
source: During early life, children exhibit heightened developmental plasticity and are more sensitive to environmental conditions than later in life (Barker, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barker, 2007

claim: The theory of developmental origins of health and disease postulates that multiple, cumulative early life exposures to adverse environmental factors may increase allostatic load and susceptibility to adult diseases.
source: The theory of developmental origins of health and disease postulates that multiple, cumulative early life exposures to adverse environmental factors may increase allostatic load (the cumulative biological damage from chronic stress) and susceptibility to adult diseases (Barker, 2007; Juster et al., 2010; Price et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by three citations to published literature

claim: Accumulating evidence implicates telomere length attrition as a potentially important underlying mechanism that links early life insults with adverse health outcomes later in life.
source: Accumulating evidence implicates telomere length (TL) attrition as a potentially important underlying mechanism that links early life insults with adverse health outcomes later in life (Price et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2013

claim: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences and protein complexes protecting the ends of linear chromosomes.
source: Telomeres, the repetitive DNA sequences and protein complexes protecting the ends of linear chromosomes, gradually shorten during normal cell division.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about telomere structure

claim: Telomeres gradually shorten during normal cell division.
source: Telomeres, the repetitive DNA sequences and protein complexes protecting the ends of linear chromosomes, gradually shorten during normal cell division.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about telomere biology

claim: Progressive telomere shortening leads to chromosome instability and cell senescence.
source: Progressive telomere shortening leads to chromosome instability and cell senescence (Blackburn, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blackburn, 2001

claim: Shorter telomere length has been linked to several age-related conditions including diabetes, heart disease, and early mortality.
source: Shorter TL has been linked to several age-related conditions including diabetes, heart disease, and early mortality (Cawthon et al., 2003; Fitzpatrick et al., 2007; Salpea et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by three citations to published literature

claim: It remains an open debate whether telomere length serves as a 'molecular clock' that gauges cumulative stress exposures over a lifespan or plays a role in the etiology of various diseases.
source: It remains an open debate whether TL serves as a 'molecular clock' that gauges cumulative stress exposures over a lifespan or plays a role in the etiology of various diseases (Blackburn et al., 2015; Hamad et al., 2016; Zhan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by three citations to published literature

claim: Acute or chronic infections may contribute to childhood telomere length attrition.
source: Acute or chronic infections may contribute to childhood TL attrition, and inflammation and oxidative stress may be potential mediators (Houben et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Houben et al., 2008

claim: Inflammation and oxidative stress may be potential mediators of infection-related telomere length attrition.
source: Acute or chronic infections may contribute to childhood TL attrition, and inflammation and oxidative stress may be potential mediators (Houben et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by citation

claim: Infections may induce T-cell proliferation and accelerated telomere attrition.
source: Infections may induce T-cell proliferation and accelerated telomere attrition (Aviv, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aviv, 2004

claim: No studies have directly investigated the relationship between infection and childhood telomere length.
source: Although no studies have directly investigated the relationship between infection and childhood TL, related studies in adults and animals support the plausibility of an association.
evidence: Statement about absence of evidence in the literature

claim: Repeated exposures to Salmonella enterica cause telomere attrition in animal models.
source: Animal models have demonstrated that repeated exposures to Salmonella enterica cause telomere attrition (Ilmonen et al., 2008), and prenatal chronic malaria infections shorten offspring TL (Asghar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ilmonen et al., 2008

claim: Prenatal chronic malaria infections shorten offspring telomere length in animal models.
source: Animal models have demonstrated that repeated exposures to Salmonella enterica cause telomere attrition (Ilmonen et al., 2008), and prenatal chronic malaria infections shorten offspring TL (Asghar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Asghar et al., 2015

claim: In adult humans, Helicobacter pylori infection, hepatitis C virus, HIV, and experimentally induced respiratory infection have been associated with shorter telomere length.
source: In adult humans, Helicobacter pylori infection, hepatitis C virus, HIV, and experimentally induced respiratory infection have been associated with shorter TL (Cohen et al., 2013; Gianesin et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2009; Zanet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by four citations to published literature

claim: Caregiver-reported diarrhea in the first two years of life predicted shorter adult telomere length.
source: Furthermore, caregiver-reported diarrhea in the first two years of life predicted shorter adult TL (Eisenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eisenberg et al., 2017

claim: Early life water, sanitation, and handwashing interventions could potentially prevent or reduce infections and slow telomere attrition.
source: Early life water, sanitation, and handwashing (WSH) interventions could potentially prevent or reduce infections and slow telomere attrition.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential intervention effects

claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of water, sanitation, and handwashing interventions reported a reduction in diarrheal illness with a pooled estimate of relative risk 0.67 (95% CI 0.59–0.76).
source: A systematic review and meta-analysis of WSH interventions reported a reduction in diarrheal illness (pooled estimate of relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.76) (Fewtrell et al., 2005), and a randomized controlled trial in Pakistan showed that promotion of handwashing decreased acute respiratory infections in children (Luby et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fewtrell et al., 2005

claim: A randomized controlled trial in Pakistan showed that promotion of handwashing decreased acute respiratory infections in children.
source: A systematic review and meta-analysis of WSH interventions reported a reduction in diarrheal illness (pooled estimate of relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.76) (Fewtrell et al., 2005), and a randomized controlled trial in Pakistan showed that promotion of handwashing decreased acute respiratory infections in children (Luby et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luby et al., 2005

claim: No studies have examined the impact of water, sanitation, and handwashing interventions on telomere length.
source: To our knowledge, no studies have examined the impact of WSH interventions on TL.
evidence: Statement about absence of evidence in the literature

claim: Early life nutrition may affect childhood telomere length.
source: Early life nutrition may affect childhood TL.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential relationship

claim: Breast milk could potentially reduce telomere attrition by protecting against inflammation and oxidative stress.
source: Breast milk could potentially reduce telomere attrition by protecting against inflammation and oxidative stress (Cacho and Lawrence, 2017; Matos et al., 2015) – exposures associated with telomere attrition (Houben et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citations

claim: Studies have found an association between exclusive breastfeeding and preschool telomere length.
source: Studies have found an association between exclusive breastfeeding and preschool TL (Wojcicki et al., 2016a), but no association with adult TL (Eisenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wojcicki et al., 2016a

claim: Studies have found no association between exclusive breastfeeding and adult telomere length.
source: Studies have found an association between exclusive breastfeeding and preschool TL (Wojcicki et al., 2016a), but no association with adult TL (Eisenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eisenberg et al., 2017

claim: Improved intake of micronutrients may promote telomere maintenance.
source: Improved intake of micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) may promote telomere maintenance (Bull and Fenech, 2008).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation

claim: Studies in adult populations have found mixed evidence for associations between telomere length, multivitamin usage, and various micronutrients.
source: Studies in adult populations have found mixed evidence for associations between TL, multivitamin usage, and various micronutrients (Cassidy et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013; Paul et al., 2015; Richards et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by five citations to published literature

claim: No randomized controlled trials have assessed the effect of nutritional interventions on child telomere length.
source: To our knowledge, no randomized controlled trials have assessed the effect of nutritional interventions on child TL.
evidence: Statement about absence of evidence in the literature

claim: Telomeres shorten fourfold faster in infants compared to adults.
source: Telomeres shorten fourfold faster in infants compared to adults (Zeichner et al., 1999); however, only a few studies have assessed the potential associations between environmental factors and TL in early childhood, a sensitive window of growth and development (Entringer et al., 2013; Marchetto et al., 2016; Theall et al., 2013a; Theall et al., 2013b; Wojcicki et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeichner et al., 1999

claim: Only a few studies have assessed the potential associations between environmental factors and telomere length in early childhood.
source: Telomeres shorten fourfold faster in infants compared to adults (Zeichner et al., 1999); however, only a few studies have assessed the potential associations between environmental factors and TL in early childhood, a sensitive window of growth and development (Entringer et al., 2013; Marchetto et al., 2016; Theall et al., 2013a; Theall et al., 2013b; Wojcicki et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by five citations to published literature

claim: The trajectories of infant telomere length in low-income countries are unknown.
source: The trajectories of infant TL in low-income countries and the potential impact of early life health-improvement interventions on TL are unknown.
evidence: Statement about absence of evidence in the literature

claim: The potential impact of early life health-improvement interventions on telomere length is unknown.
source: The trajectories of infant TL in low-income countries and the potential impact of early life health-improvement interventions on TL are unknown.
evidence: Statement about absence of evidence in the literature

claim: Between May 2012 and July 2013, 720 geographical clusters of 5551 pregnant women were randomized to a control or an intervention arm in the overall trial.
source: Between May 2012 and July 2013, in the overall trial, we randomized 720 geographical clusters of 5551 pregnant women to a control or an intervention arm.
evidence: Direct statement about trial enrollment and randomization

claim: In the substudy, after 1 year of intervention, 662 children were assessed (341 intervention and 321 control).
source: In this substudy, after 1 year of intervention, we assessed a total of 662 children (341 intervention and 321 control) and 713 children after 2 years of intervention (383 intervention and 330 control).
evidence: Direct statement about substudy sample sizes

claim: In the substudy, after 2 years of intervention, 713 children were assessed (383 intervention and 330 control).
source: In this substudy, after 1 year of intervention, we assessed a total of 662 children (341 intervention and 321 control) and 713 children after 2 years of intervention (383 intervention and 330 control).
evidence: Direct statement about substudy sample sizes

claim: Children in the intervention arm had significantly shorter relative telomere length compared with controls after 1 year of intervention (difference −163 base pairs, p=0.001).
source: Children in the intervention arm had significantly shorter relative TL compared with controls after 1 year of intervention (difference −163 base pairs (bp), p=0.001).
evidence: Direct statement of primary outcome with statistical significance

claim: Between years 1 and 2, telomere length increased in the intervention arm (+76 bp) and decreased in the controls (−23 bp) (p=0.050).
source: Between years 1 and 2, TL increased in the intervention arm (+76 bp) and decreased in the controls (−23 bp) (p=0.050).
evidence: Direct statement of change in telomere length with statistical significance

claim: After 2 years, there was no difference in telomere length between the intervention and control arms (p=0.305).
source: After 2 years, there was no difference between the arms (p=0.305).
evidence: Direct statement of outcome with statistical significance

claim: The unexpected finding of increased telomere attrition during the first year of life in the intervention group suggests that rapid telomere attrition during this critical period could reflect improved growth in the intervention group, rather than accumulated stress.
source: Our unexpected finding of increased telomere attrition during the first year of life in the intervention group suggests that rapid telomere attrition during this critical period could reflect the improved growth in the intervention group, rather than accumulated stress.
evidence: Interpretive statement based on study findings

claim: Between 31 May 2012 and 7 July 2013, 5551 compounds with pregnant women in their first or second trimester were randomly allocated to one of six intervention groups or a double sized control group.
source: Between 31 May 2012 and 7 July 2013, in the overall trial, 5551 compounds (collections of related households) with pregnant women in their first or second trimester were randomly allocated to one of the six intervention groups or a double sized control group as follows: (1) chlorinated drinking water and safe storage vessel, (2) upgraded sanitation (child potties, sani-scoop hoes to remove feces, and a double pit latrine with a hygienic water seal), (3) handwashing promotion (handwashing stations with detergent soap), (4) combined water + sanitation + handwashing (5) nutrition (lipid-based nutrient supplements and age-appropriate recommendations on maternal nutrition and infant feeding practices), (6) combined nutrition + water + sanitation + handwashing (N + WSH), (7) control group, which did not receive any interventions (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about trial enrollment and randomization

claim: Community health promoters visited study compounds in the intervention arms to promote behaviors.
source: Community health promoters visited study compounds in the intervention arms to promote behaviors.
evidence: Direct statement about intervention delivery

claim: The substudy team visited 996 index children after 1 year of intervention and 1021 children after 2 years of intervention in the control and N + WSH arms only.
source: The substudy team visited 996 index children after 1 year of intervention (Y1) and 1021 children after 2 years of intervention (Y2) in the control and N + WSH arms only.
evidence: Direct statement about substudy sample sizes

claim: Telomere length outcomes were measured in 66.5% of the children (N = 662) at Year 1 and 69.8% of the children (N = 713) at Year 2.
source: TL outcomes were measured in 66.5% of the children (N = 662) at Y1% and 69.8% of the children (N = 713) at Y2, but not at birth (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about outcome measurement rates

claim: Telomere length was not measured at birth.
source: TL outcomes were measured in 66.5% of the children (N = 662) at Y1% and 69.8% of the children (N = 713) at Y2, but not at birth (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about measurement timing

claim: Telomere length at birth is expected to be similar for the intervention and control arms because household enrollment characteristics were balanced between both arms.
source: We expect TL at birth to be similar for the intervention and control arms because household enrollment characteristics were balanced between both arms (Table 1).
evidence: Inference based on randomization and balance of baseline characteristics

claim: At the time of telomere length assessment, the mean age was 14.1 (±2.1) months at Year 1 and 28.2 (±1.9) months at Year 2.
source: At the time of TL assessment, the mean (±SD) age was 14.1 (±2.1) months at Y1 and 28.2 (±1.9) months at Y2.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data

claim: Telomere length was normally distributed.
source: TL was normally distributed (Figure 2).
evidence: Statement supported by reference to Figure 2

claim: The mean telomere length was 1.43 (±0.23) T/S ratio at Year 1 (6729 ± 549 base pairs) and 1.45 (±0.24) T/S ratio at Year 2 (6763 ± 586 bp).
source: The mean (±SD) TL was 1.43 (±0.23) T/S ratio at Y1 (6729 ± 549 base pairs (bp)) and 1.45 (±0.24) T/S ratio at Y2 (6763 ± 586 bp).
evidence: Direct statement of measured data

claim: The average telomere lengths in this study are short for young children compared to some previous findings.
source: Although these averages are short for young children compared to some previous findings (Factor-Litvak et al., 2016; Frenck et al., 1998; Wojcicki et al., 2016a), they are similar to a recent report of newborns whose mothers experienced a high level of stress during pregnancy (Marchetto et al., 2016); the stress associated with low socioeconomic status may have contributed to the short average TL in this study.
evidence: Comparison to published literature supported by citations

claim: The average telomere lengths in this study are similar to a recent report of newborns whose mothers experienced a high level of stress during pregnancy.
source: Although these averages are short for young children compared to some previous findings (Factor-Litvak et al., 2016; Frenck et al., 1998; Wojcicki et al., 2016a), they are similar to a recent report of newborns whose mothers experienced a high level of stress during pregnancy (Marchetto et al., 2016); the stress associated with low socioeconomic status may have contributed to the short average TL in this study.
evidence: Comparison to published literature supported by citation

claim: The stress associated with low socioeconomic status may have contributed to the short average telomere length in this study.
source: Although these averages are short for young children compared to some previous findings (Factor-Litvak et al., 2016; Frenck et al., 1998; Wojcicki et al., 2016a), they are similar to a recent report of newborns whose mothers experienced a high level of stress during pregnancy (Marchetto et al., 2016); the stress associated with low socioeconomic status may have contributed to the short average TL in this study.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings

claim: Measures of intervention adherence were high (over 80%) and sustained throughout Year 1 and Year 2.
source: Measures of intervention adherence (including observed hardware availability) were high (over 80%) and sustained throughout Y1 and Y2 (S. P. Luby et al. in review).
evidence: Direct statement about measured adherence data

claim: After 1 year of intervention, compared with controls (mean = 1.47 T/S or 6813 bp), children in the combined intervention arm (mean = 1.40 T/S or 6650 bp) had significantly shorter relative telomere length (difference −0.07 T/S or −163 bp, p=0.001).
source: After 1 year of intervention, compared with controls (mean = 1.47 T/S or 6813 bp), children in the combined intervention arm (mean = 1.40 T/S or 6650 bp) had significantly shorter relative TL (difference −0.07 T/S or −163 bp, p=0.001; Table 3).
evidence: Direct statement of primary outcome with statistical significance

claim: The entire distribution of the T/S ratio was shifted lower for the intervention arm compared to the control at Year 1.
source: The entire distribution of the T/S ratio was shifted lower for the intervention arm compared to the control at Y1 (Figure 2).
evidence: Statement supported by reference to Figure 2

claim: Unadjusted, adjusted, and inverse probability of censoring weighting analyses yielded similar estimates for the Year 1 telomere length difference.
source: Unadjusted, adjusted, and inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW; to adjust for potential bias from loss to follow-up) analyses yielded similar estimates (Table 3).
evidence: Statement about consistency of statistical analyses

claim: At the Year 2 measurement, there was no significant difference (p=0.305) between the intervention arm and the control.
source: At the Y2 measurement, there was no significant difference (p=0.305) between the intervention arm and the control (Table 3, Figure 2).
evidence: Direct statement of outcome with statistical significance

claim: Of index children with a telomere length measurement at both Year 1 and Year 2 (N = 557; 54.6% of the total children visited), relative telomere length increased by +0.03 T/S (+76 bp) in the intervention group and decreased by −0.01 T/S (−23 bp) in the control group.
source: Of index children with a TL measurement at both Y1 and Y2 (N = 557; 54.6% of the total children visited), relative TL increased by +0.03 T/S (+76 bp) in the intervention group and decreased by −0.01 T/S (−23 bp) in the control group (Table 3).
evidence: Direct statement of measured change in telomere length

claim: The difference between the control and intervention arms in the change in relative telomere length from Year 1 to Year 2 was 0.04 T/S and was borderline significant (p=0.050).
source: Overall, the difference between the control and intervention arms in the change in relative TL from Y1 to Y2 was 0.04 T/S and was borderline significant (p=0.050; Table 3).
evidence: Direct statement of outcome with statistical significance

claim: Unadjusted, adjusted, and inverse probability of censoring weighting analyses generated similar estimates for the change in telomere length from Year 1 to Year 2, but only the unadjusted model was significant.
source: Unadjusted, adjusted, and inverse probability of censoring weighting analyses generated similar estimates but only the unadjusted model was significant (Table 3).
evidence: Statement about consistency and significance of statistical analyses

claim: Sex was not a significant effect modifier (sex by treatment interaction p=0.435 at Year 1 and p=0.105 at Year 2).
source: Sex was not a significant effect modifier (sex by treatment interaction p=0.435 at Y1 and p=0.105 at Y2; Table 4).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result

claim: Boys had shorter telomere length than girls at Year 1 (−0.07 T/S, p=0.007) and Year 2 (−0.09 T/S, p=0.001).
source: Boys had shorter TL than girls at Y1 (−0.07 T/S, p=0.007) and Y2 (−0.09 T/S, p=0.001), consistent with previous studies (Gardner et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement of measured data with statistical significance

claim: The finding that boys had shorter telomere length than girls is consistent with previous studies.
source: Boys had shorter TL than girls at Y1 (−0.07 T/S, p=0.007) and Y2 (−0.09 T/S, p=0.001), consistent with previous studies (Gardner et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to published literature supported by citation

claim: Seasonal variation in telomere length was not observed within this study.
source: Although a previous study reported seasonal variation in TL (Rehkopf et al., 2014), we did not observe seasonal changes within this study.
evidence: Direct statement of study findings

claim: The accelerated telomere length attrition observed during the first year of life in the intervention arm may reflect improved immune system development.
source: The accelerated TL attrition observed during the first year of life in the intervention arm may reflect improved immune system development.
evidence: Interpretive speculation about study findings

claim: The WASH Benefits trial found that children in the intervention arm had reductions in caregiver-reported diarrhea, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and Giardia duodenalis infections compared with the control arm.
source: The WASH Benefits trial found that children in the intervention arm had reductions in caregiver-reported diarrhea, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and Giardia duodenalis infections compared with the control arm (S. P. Luby et al., A. Ercumen et al., and A. Lin et al. in review).
evidence: Statement about trial findings supported by citations to manuscripts in review

claim: It is plausible that the interventions improved immune system development resulting in subsequent protection against infections.
source: It is plausible that the interventions improved immune system development resulting in subsequent protection against infections or that the decreased exposure to pathogens may have improved immunity.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of potential mechanisms

claim: The decreased exposure to pathogens may have improved immunity.
source: It is plausible that the interventions improved immune system development resulting in subsequent protection against infections or that the decreased exposure to pathogens may have improved immunity.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of potential mechanisms

claim: The concept of accelerated telomere length attrition during the first year of life as a reflection of better immune system development is consistent with studies that have reported rapid telomere attrition and accelerated differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells during the first year of life.
source: The concept of accelerated TL attrition during the first year of life as a reflection of better immune system development is consistent with studies that have reported rapid telomere attrition and accelerated differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), stem cells that give rise to all lineages of immune cells, during the first year of life.
evidence: Interpretive statement connecting study findings to published literature

claim: A healthy individual experiences approximately 17 hematopoietic stem cell divisions in the first year of life, followed by approximately 2.5 divisions/year between ages 3–13 years, and approximately 0.6 divisions/year in adults.
source: A healthy individual experiences ~ 17 HSC divisions in the first year of life, followed by ~2.5 divisions/year between ages 3–13 years, and ~0.6 divisions/year in adults (Elwood, 2004; Kimura et al., 2010; Rufer et al., 1999; Sidorov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by four citations to published literature

claim: Telomere length shortens in proportion to the number of cell replications.
source: Since TL shortens in proportion to the number of cell replications, HSC progenitor divisions correspond with TL attrition rates (Elwood, 2004; Kimura et al., 2010; Rufer et al., 1999; Sidorov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by four citations to published literature

claim: Hematopoietic stem cell progenitor divisions correspond with telomere length attrition rates.
source: Since TL shortens in proportion to the number of cell replications, HSC progenitor divisions correspond with TL attrition rates (Elwood, 2004; Kimura et al., 2010; Rufer et al., 1999; Sidorov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by four citations to published literature

claim: In the first year of life, children in the control group with poor immune system development would potentially experience less hematopoietic stem cell divisions and slower rates of telomere length attrition compared to the intervention group.
source: In the first year of life, children in the control group with poor immune system development would potentially experience less HSC divisions and slower rates of TL attrition compared to the intervention group.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from cited literature

claim: The accelerated telomere length attrition during the first year of life in the intervention arm may also reflect better linear growth.
source: The accelerated TL attrition during the first year of life in the intervention arm may also reflect better linear growth.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of study findings

claim: The intervention improved child linear growth at both Year 1 and Year 2 measurements.
source: The intervention improved child linear growth at both Y1 and Y2 measurements (S. P. Luby et al. in review).
evidence: Statement about trial findings supported by citation to manuscript in review

claim: An evolutionary adaptation of organisms during infections is to restrict growth, and instead redirect nutrients and energy to ensure survival.
source: An evolutionary adaptation of organisms during infections is to restrict growth, and instead redirect nutrients and energy to ensure survival (O'Connor et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Connor et al., 2008

claim: The decreased pathogen exposure and the subsequent reduction in acquired infections are potential mechanisms by which better growth was attained in the intervention arm.
source: We postulate that the decreased pathogen exposure and the subsequent reduction in acquired infections are potential mechanisms by which better growth was attained in the intervention arm.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of potential mechanisms

claim: Some studies have reported high synchrony between peripheral blood and telomere length attrition rates within other somatic tissues in the same individual.
source: Some studies have reported high synchrony between peripheral blood and TL attrition rates within other somatic tissues in the same individual (Daniali et al., 2013; Takubo et al., 2002), while others have found differences (Dlouha et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by two citations to published literature

claim: Some studies have found differences between peripheral blood and telomere length attrition rates within other somatic tissues in the same individual.
source: Some studies have reported high synchrony between peripheral blood and TL attrition rates within other somatic tissues in the same individual (Daniali et al., 2013; Takubo et al., 2002), while others have found differences (Dlouha et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by two citations to published literature

claim: The accelerated peripheral blood telomere length attrition in the intervention group during the first year of life could potentially indicate rapid muscle or bone cell division involved in growth.
source: Although the results of these prior investigations are equivocal, the accelerated peripheral blood TL attrition in the intervention group during the first year of life could potentially indicate rapid muscle or bone cell division involved in growth.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference

claim: Early life telomere length may be a proxy measure for growth and development of the immune system, the brain, and other vital tissues.
source: We hypothesize that early life TL may be a proxy measure for growth and development of the immune system, the brain, and other vital tissues.
evidence: Explicit hypothesis statement

claim: The borderline significant finding that telomere length increased in the intervention arm and decreased in the control arm from Year 1 to Year 2 seems to represent a preview of the telomere length trajectories that are set.
source: After the initial period of rapid linear growth during Y1, our borderline significant finding that telomere length increased in the intervention arm and decreased in the control arm from Y1 to Y2 seems to represent a preview of the TL trajectories that are set: we hypothesize that the intervention children will experience slower lifetime TL attrition and more physiological resistance to stress-related diseases (Juster et al., 2010).
evidence: Interpretive speculation about study findings

claim: The intervention children are hypothesized to experience slower lifetime telomere length attrition and more physiological resistance to stress-related diseases.
source: After the initial period of rapid linear growth during Y1, our borderline significant finding that telomere length increased in the intervention arm and decreased in the control arm from Y1 to Y2 seems to represent a preview of the TL trajectories that are set: we hypothesize that the intervention children will experience slower lifetime TL attrition and more physiological resistance to stress-related diseases (Juster et al., 2010).
evidence: Explicit hypothesis statement supported by citation

claim: The change in relative telomere length from Year 1 to Year 2 was small (0.04 T/S 95% confidence interval 0.00, 0.08) and the p-value borderline (p=0.050).
source: The change in relative TL from Y1 to Y2 was small (0.04 T/S 95% confidence interval 0.00, 0.08) and the p-value borderline (p=0.050).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical results

claim: The diarrhea, soil-transmitted helminth, Giardia duodenalis, and growth results suggest that these interventions are potentially interrupting key infection and malnutrition pathways to reduce exposure to biological adversity and allostatic load.
source: Nevertheless, our diarrhea, soil-transmitted helminth, Giardia duodenalis, and growth results suggest that these interventions are potentially interrupting key infection and malnutrition pathways to reduce exposure to biological adversity and allostatic load (S. P. Luby et al., A. Ercumen et al., and A. Lin et al. in review).
evidence: Interpretive statement based on study findings supported by citations

claim: In a Filipino cohort, decreased infant diarrheal prevalence was associated with longer adult telomere length.
source: In a Filipino cohort, decreased infant diarrheal prevalence was associated with longer adult TL (Eisenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eisenberg et al., 2017

claim: In observational studies, various vitamins were associated with longer adult telomere length.
source: In observational studies, various vitamins were associated with longer adult TL (Xu et al., 2009), and early exclusive breastfeeding was associated with longer child TL at ages 4–5 years (Wojcicki et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2009

claim: Early exclusive breastfeeding was associated with longer child telomere length at ages 4–5 years.
source: In observational studies, various vitamins were associated with longer adult TL (Xu et al., 2009), and early exclusive breastfeeding was associated with longer child TL at ages 4–5 years (Wojcicki et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wojcicki et al., 2016a

claim: The nutrition intervention included promotion of exclusive breastfeeding and micronutrient fortified lipid-based nutrient supplements.
source: Our nutrition intervention included promotion of exclusive breastfeeding and micronutrient fortified lipid-based nutrient supplements.

claim: The Year 1 to Year 2 changes in telomere length that were observed are consistent with studies showing associations between nutrition and telomere length.
source: The Y1 to Y2 changes in TL that we observed are consistent with these studies.

claim: The smaller than expected treatment effect and the borderline p-value indicate that the trial was slightly underpowered to detect differences in the change in relative telomere length from Year 1 to Year 2 among the intervention and control groups.
source: The smaller than expected treatment effect and the borderline p-value indicate that the trial was slightly underpowered to detect differences in the change in relative TL from Y1 to Y2 among the intervention and control groups.
evidence: Interpretive statement about statistical power based on study results

claim: The finding of a modest, borderline impact from Year 1 to Year 2 may suggest that the effect of the interventions is diminished in children over 1 year of age.
